title: A claims portal's requirements: a conflict, a baseline over capacity, a withheld signature and a change

objective: Obtaining sign-off on the requirements baseline through decision-making techniques that build stakeholder consensus
secondaryObjectives: Allocating accepted/deferred requirements against scope, schedule, budget, and resource constraints to create a requirements baseline
Evaluating product options and capabilities with decision-making and valuation techniques to accept, defer, or reject requirements
Managing requirement changes by assessing impact, dependencies, and risk against the change-control plan and requirements baseline

sources.cite: PMI, Professional in Business Analysis (PMI-PBA) exam: Needs Assessment 18%, Planning 22%, Analysis 35%, Traceability and Monitoring 15%, Evaluation 10%

sources.cite: Jama Software, Requirements Management Guide: Defining and Implementing a Requirements Baseline (page modified 2026-10-02)
sources.note: Read 2026-11-17 through a summarizing fetch. A requirements baseline is 'a snapshot in time that represents an agreed-upon, reviewed, and approved set of requirements' committed to a release; stakeholders who sign off are 'agreeing and committing to a specific requirements baseline'; 'Change requests are made against an established baseline'; before baselining, confirm 'that the change control board is assembled and chartered'. A vendor's guide, cited for the practice, not as a standard.

brief.situation: You are the business analyst for Lakeview Mutual, a fictional insurer, on release 1 of its online claims portal. The project is predictive: 10 weeks and 200 thousand dollars, with the requirements baselined and signed off by the end of week 5. The claims and finance directors sign the baseline; the sponsor decides if they disagree.
handover: Sponsor: Priya Nair, chief operating officer. Claims director: Tom Becker. Finance director: Ana Morales.
Planned value is 20 thousand dollars a week; the dashboard shows PV, EV, AC, SPI and CPI at each Friday status meeting.
howItWorks: The dashboard shows the release objective and plan, the requirement groups by state, earned value against plan, the open issues, the people and the milestones.
Move the project on a week at a time. Decisions come to you as they arise; before them you can review the traceability matrix or demonstrate the prototype.
At go-live you close the release and write a short note.

trace.label: Review the traceability matrix
trace.available: not busy and phase == "build" and isNull(traceAt)
trace.why: Done, or finish what you are doing first.

effects.log: You walk the matrix from business objectives to requirements to tests.

effects.finding: Every intake and adjuster requirement traces to an objective; the 9 dashboards trace to Finance's 'should' list; the 6 reserve reports trace to the regulator's rule. A change to the claim record touches 2 adjuster screens and 2 tests.

proto.label: Demonstrate the clickable prototype to both directors
proto.available: not busy and phase == "build" and isNull(protoAt)
proto.why: Done, or finish what you are doing first.

effects.log: You walk both directors through the prototype screens against the requirements.

effects.finding: Both agree the screens match the requirements; Finance notices the trend report is not there and says it is a 'nice to have for now'.

options.label: Update the traceability matrix and baseline to v1.1 (with CR-04), list the deferred requirements for release 2, and archive the sign-off record
Hand over to support and start release 2

then.log: Developers build the payout flow twice, once for each department's rule.
Overtime to fit 42 requirements into capacity for 33.
Compliance review: the regulator's reserve reports are required for go-live. They go back in, late.
Finance rejects the built reports it never signed off; two weeks of reporting work is redone.
The trend report, added to win a signature, was never sized; the team absorbs it.
The fraud field breaks two adjuster screens nobody traced to it.
CR-04 built in three days as analyzed; the trace and tests updated.

else.log: Friday of week 10: release 1 goes live.

effects.log: End of week 2: two directors, two rules.
End of week 4: the analyzed requirements are sized.
End of week 5: sign-off is due.
End of week 8: a request from Claims.

conflictPrompt.title: End of week 2: conflicting requirements
conflictPrompt.context: Claims wants payouts under 500 dollars paid instantly; Finance wants every payout approved by an adjuster. Both are written as must-haves. The developers need one rule.

choices.label: Run a prioritization workshop with both directors: score the options against the release objective and the fraud risk, agree one rule (instant under 500 dollars with an automated fraud check), and record the rationale

effects.log: One rule, agreed and recorded with its rationale.

choices.feedback: Conflicting requirements are resolved with a decision-making technique against agreed criteria, and the rationale is recorded.

choices.label: Keep both as must-haves; the developers can make it configurable
choices.feedback: Two contradictory must-haves are not a requirement; they move the conflict to the developers.

choices.label: Take Claims' version; the claims director is the louder voice and more senior

effects.log: Finance is overruled without a hearing.

choices.feedback: Deciding by seniority or volume skips the agreed decision process and loses the overruled stakeholder.

allocPrompt.title: End of week 4: 42 requirements, capacity for 33
allocPrompt.context: Analysis gives 42 must and should requirements; the team's capacity to week 10 is about 33. The 6 reserve reports are required by the regulator. The 9 trend dashboards are Finance's 'should'.

choices.label: Allocate against the constraints: baseline the 33 must-haves (with the reserve reports) for release 1, defer the 9 dashboards to release 2 with their trace, and say so to Finance

effects.log: Release 1 fits capacity; the deferred list is traced.

choices.feedback: Accepted requirements are allocated against scope, schedule, budget and resources; what does not fit is deferred, not dropped, and stays traced.

choices.label: Baseline all 42 and plan overtime

effects.log: All 42 go in; overtime from week 6.

choices.feedback: A baseline that exceeds capacity is a plan to overrun.

choices.label: Cut the reserve reports to fit; they are only back-office
choices.feedback: A requirement traced to a regulation is a constraint, not a candidate for deferral.

signPrompt.title: End of week 5: the finance director will not sign
signPrompt.context: The claims director has signed the baseline. The finance director says: "I won't sign without a trend report." Build starts Monday. The plan says the sponsor decides if the directors disagree.

choices.label: Walk the finance director through the baseline on the prototype, log the trend report as a release-2 request, and if she still objects take it to the sponsor as the plan says; record the sign-off

effects.log: Signed: the trend report is a logged request for release 2.

choices.feedback: Sign-off is reached with the plan's decision rule: validate the baseline with the stakeholder, record the open request, escalate per the plan if needed.

choices.label: Start the build Monday without her signature; it can be fixed later

effects.log: Build starts on an unsigned baseline.

choices.feedback: Building on an unsigned baseline is building on requirements nobody has committed to.

choices.label: Add the trend report to the baseline to get her signature

effects.log: The trend report goes in unsized; she signs.

choices.feedback: Adding scope to win a signature skips the analysis and the allocation.

crPrompt.title: End of week 8: a change after sign-off
crPrompt.context: The claims director asks for a fraud score on each claim, shown in the adjuster queue: "It's one field." The baseline is signed; the plan routes changes to the change control board with an impact analysis.

choices.label: Log CR-04, trace its impact (the claim record, 2 adjuster screens, 2 tests: about 3 days), and take it to the change control board

effects.log: The board approves CR-04 with its impact known; baseline v1.1.

choices.feedback: A change against the baseline is assessed for impact, dependencies and risk through the trace, and decided by the change control board.

choices.label: Ask a developer to add the field; it is small

effects.log: The field goes in on request.

choices.feedback: A small change outside change control is still a change: here it broke two screens nobody traced.

choices.label: Refuse: the baseline is frozen

effects.log: Claims is told no without an analysis.

choices.feedback: A baseline is controlled, not frozen; a change request is analyzed and decided.

reflection.question: Write the release note for the sponsor: how the baseline was built and signed, and how the conflict and the change after sign-off were handled.

parts.label: Baseline and sign-off
parts.criteria: Resolves the conflict with agreed criteria and a recorded rationale; allocates against capacity with the regulator's reports kept and the dashboards deferred and traced; reaches sign-off by the plan's decision rule.
parts.modelAnswer: One payout rule came out of a scored workshop. The baseline held the 33 must-haves, including the regulator's reserve reports, and deferred 9 dashboards with their trace. Finance signed after the prototype walk-through, with the trend report logged for release 2.

parts.label: Change after sign-off
parts.criteria: Treats the fraud field as a change request: impact through the trace, decided by the change control board, baseline versioned.
parts.modelAnswer: CR-04 touched the claim record, two adjuster screens and two tests: about three days. The board approved it and the baseline became v1.1.

baselined.headline: Good: baselined, signed and controlled
baselined.body: The conflict was decided on criteria, the baseline fit capacity, sign-off followed the plan and the change went through the board.

scoring.modelReasoning: Conflicting requirements are decided with a technique the stakeholders agree to, scored against the business objectives, and the rationale is recorded. Accepted requirements are allocated against capacity, budget and schedule into a baseline; what does not fit is deferred and stays traced, and a requirement traced to a regulation stays in. Sign-off is reached with the decision rule in the requirements management plan: validate the baseline with the objecting stakeholder (a prototype helps), log the new ask as a request, and escalate to the sponsor if needed. After sign-off the baseline is controlled, not frozen: a change is logged, its impact traced through dependencies and tests, and the change control board decides.
